# Overview

`shapvalues` computes Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) for the predictions
of any supervised model through a single prediction callback. It covers
regression, binary and multiclass classification, and right-censored survival
analysis with time-dependent attributions.

The estimator is the sampling (permutation) estimator of
Strumbelj and Kononenko (2014). Two implementation choices make it fast:

1. every coalition prediction needed for a batch of observations is assembled
   into **one data frame and scored in a single call** to the prediction
   callback, so the per-call overhead of the model is paid once instead of
   thousands of times;
2. the marginal-contribution reduction over those predictions runs in
   **parallel C++** via `RcppParallel`.

The same background rows are reused across all explained observations, which
makes the Monte Carlo estimate satisfy *local accuracy* exactly (up to
floating point) and acts as a common-random-numbers variance reduction.

This vignette states the estimand and the estimator for every method the
package implements, then shows the API on worked examples. It is a more
detailed companion to the package `README`.

# The Shapley value

Let $f$ be the quantity we explain: a regression function, a class
probability, or a survival probability at a fixed time. For an instance
$x$ with $p$ features indexed by $F = \{1, \dots, p\}$, write $v(S)$ for the
model output when only the features in $S \subseteq F$ are "present" and the
rest are integrated out over a background distribution:
$$
v(S) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[\, f\big(x_S,\; z_{F \setminus S}\big) \right],
$$
where $x_S$ are the values of $x$ on $S$ and $z_{F\setminus S}$ is drawn from
the background data. The Shapley value of feature $i$ is the average marginal
contribution of $i$ over all orderings of the features:
$$
\phi_i \;=\; \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{i\}}
\frac{|S|!\,(p - |S| - 1)!}{p!}
\Big[\, v\big(S \cup \{i\}\big) - v(S) \,\Big].
$$
It is the unique attribution that is efficient, symmetric, null-player and
linear. *Efficiency* is the local-accuracy property used throughout the
package:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i \;=\; v(F) - v(\varnothing)
\;=\; f(x) - \mathbb{E}_z[f(z)].
$$
The right-most term $\mathbb{E}_z[f(z)]$ is the **baseline** returned in
`sv$baseline`.

# The permutation (sampling) estimator

The exact sum over subsets costs $2^p$ evaluations. The sampling estimator
rewrites $\phi_i$ as an expectation over a uniformly random permutation
$\pi$ of the features:
$$
\phi_i \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,
v\big(P_i^{\pi} \cup \{i\}\big) - v\big(P_i^{\pi}\big) \right],
\qquad
P_i^{\pi} = \{\, j : \pi(j) < \pi(i) \,\},
$$
where $P_i^{\pi}$ is the set of features that precede $i$ in $\pi$. Drawing
`nsim` permutations $\pi^{(1)}, \dots, \pi^{(M)}$ and, for each, one background
row $z^{(m)}$, the estimator is
$$
\hat{\phi}_i \;=\; \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M}
\Big[\, \hat v\big(P_i^{\pi^{(m)}} \cup \{i\};\, z^{(m)}\big)
      - \hat v\big(P_i^{\pi^{(m)}};\, z^{(m)}\big) \Big],
$$
with $\hat v(S; z) = f(x_S, z_{F \setminus S})$ a single-draw estimate of the
conditioning expectation. Two details in the implementation:

* **Telescoping.** Along one permutation, the $p$ successive coalitions
  $\varnothing \subset \{\pi^{-1}(1)\} \subset \dots \subset F$ give all $p$
  feature contributions from $p + 1$ predictions, and consecutive
  differences telescope so that $\sum_i \hat\phi_i^{(m)} = f(x) - f(z^{(m)})$
  for every single permutation. Averaging preserves this, so
  `rowSums(sv$phi) + sv$baseline` equals `sv$prediction` exactly.
* **Antithetic permutations** (`antithetic = TRUE`). Permutations are drawn
  in reversed pairs $(\pi, \pi^{\text{rev}})$. The two orderings are
  negatively correlated, which lowers the variance of $\hat\phi_i$ at no
  extra model calls; `nsim` is rounded up to an even number.

For an additive model $f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_j g_j(x_j)$ the estimator is
*exact* for any single permutation, so with `nsim >= bg_size` the result
matches the closed form to machine precision.

## Cost and batching

One explained observation costs $M (p + 1)$ predictions; a data set of $n$
rows costs $n M (p + 1)$. Rather than issue them one at a time, `shapvalues`
builds the entire $n M (p + 1) \times p$ design of coalition rows and calls
`pred_fun` once. The C++ reduction then forms the $M$ telescoping differences
per observation and averages them, parallelised over observations (and over
outputs for multi-output models) with `nthreads` threads.

# Getting started

```{r quickstart}
library(shapvalues)

fit <- lm(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
sv  <- shapvalues(fit, X = mtcars[, -1], bg = mtcars[, -1], nsim = 100)
sv
```

`shapvalues()` needs three things: a model, the rows to explain `X`, and a
background sample `bg` used to integrate out absent features. When the model
class is recognised (`lm`, `glm`, `ranger`, `xgb.Booster`) the prediction
callback is chosen automatically; otherwise pass `pred_fun`, a function with
signature `function(object, newdata)` (plus `times` for survival).

Local accuracy holds for the Monte Carlo estimate:

```{r localacc}
max(abs(rowSums(sv$phi) + sv$baseline - sv$prediction[, 1]))
```

The return value stores the attribution array `phi` (`n x p`, or
`n x p x n_output`), the `baseline` $\mathbb{E}_z[f(z)]$, the model
`prediction`, and the explained `feature_values`.

## Tables

```{r tables}
head(svtable(sv))
svimportancetable(sv)
```

# Plots

All plots are produced through the `plot()` method with a `type` argument and
return a plain `ggplot` object, so they can be themed with any
`ggplot2::theme_*()` via `+`. The gallery below uses a random forest on the
Boston housing data.

```{r boston, eval = have_gallery}
data(Boston, package = "MASS")
rf  <- ranger::ranger(medv ~ ., data = Boston, num.trees = 400)
pf  <- function(object, newdata) predict(object, newdata)$predictions
expl <- Boston[sample(nrow(Boston), 150), ]        # rows to explain
svb  <- shapvalues(rf, X = expl[, -14], bg = Boston[, -14],
                   pred_fun = pf, nsim = 60, bg_size = 200)
```

**Beeswarm** — one point per observation and feature, positioned by its SHAP
value and coloured by the (scaled) feature value.

```{r beeswarm, eval = have_gallery}
plot(svb, type = "beeswarm")
```

**Importance** — features ranked by mean absolute SHAP,
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} |\phi_{ki}|$.

```{r importance, eval = have_gallery, fig.height = 3.4}
plot(svb, type = "importance")
```

**Waterfall** — the additive decomposition for one row: starting at the
baseline $\mathbb{E}_z[f(z)]$, each bar adds one $\phi_{ki}$ and the total
lands on $f(x_k)$.

```{r waterfall, eval = have_gallery}
plot(svb, type = "waterfall", row = 1)
```

**Dependence** — $\phi_{ki}$ against the value of feature $i$, optionally
coloured by a second feature to expose interactions.

```{r dependence, eval = have_gallery}
plot(svb, type = "dependence", feature = "rm", colour_by = "lstat")
```

# Pairwise interaction values

With `interactions = TRUE`, `shapvalues()` also estimates the pairwise SHAP
interaction matrix. For a pair $(i, j)$ the interaction is the halved,
symmetrised Grabisch-Roubens Shapley interaction index (Lundberg et al.,
2020):
$$
\Phi_{ij} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,
\mathbb{E}_{s,\,S}\!\left[\,
v\big(S \cup \{i, j\}\big) - v\big(S \cup \{i\}\big)
- v\big(S \cup \{j\}\big) + v(S) \right],
$$
where $s$ is uniform on $\{0, \dots, p - 2\}$ and, given $s$, the set $S$ is a
uniform size-$s$ subset of $F \setminus \{i, j\}$. The four coalitions per
sample are scored together in the shared batched call. The diagonal is set to
the residual main effect,
$$
\Phi_{ii} \;=\; \phi_i - \sum_{j \neq i} \Phi_{ij},
$$
so every row of the $p \times p$ matrix sums to the SHAP value $\phi_i$ and
the whole matrix sums to $f(x) - \mathbb{E}_z[f(z)]$. Interaction estimation
is single-output only and costs $O(p^2)$ more predictions.

```{r interaction}
svi <- shapvalues(
  lm(mpg ~ wt * hp + disp + drat + qsec, data = mtcars),
  mtcars[, c("wt", "hp", "disp", "drat", "qsec")],
  mtcars[, c("wt", "hp", "disp", "drat", "qsec")],
  nsim = 120, interactions = TRUE
)
dim(svi$interactions)
round(svi$interactions[1, , ], 3)
```

```{r interaction-plot, eval = have_gallery}
plot(svi, type = "interaction", feature = "wt", interact = "hp")
```

# Survival: time-dependent attributions

For right-censored survival models the explained quantity is the predicted
survival probability at a set of times, $f_t(x) = \hat S(t \mid x)$. The
callback returns an $n \times |\text{times}|$ matrix, and `shapvalues()`
runs the permutation estimator independently for each column, giving an
attribution surface
$$
\phi_i(t), \qquad t \in \texttt{times},
$$
with $\sum_i \phi_i(t) = \hat S(t \mid x) - \mathbb{E}_z[\hat S(t \mid z)]$ at
every $t$. This is the SurvSHAP(t) explanation of Krzyzinski et al. (2023).

```{r survival, eval = have_surv}
library(survival)
cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + karno + celltype,
             data = veteran, x = TRUE)
pf_surv <- function(object, newdata, times) {
  s <- summary(survfit(object, newdata = newdata),
               times = times, extend = TRUE)$surv
  t(matrix(s, nrow = length(times)))
}
svs <- shapvalues(cox, veteran[, c("age", "karno", "celltype")],
                  veteran[, c("age", "karno", "celltype")],
                  pred_fun = pf_surv, times = c(30, 90, 180, 270, 365),
                  task = "survival", nsim = 60)
plot(svs, type = "surv", row = 1)
```

# Multivariate attribution views

These summarise the whole attribution vector of an observation rather than
marginalising one feature at a time.

## Compass and explanation concentration

Place unit vectors $u_1, \dots, u_p$ evenly around a circle, one per feature
(or feature group). The attribution barycentre of observation $k$ is
$$
C_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i} |\phi_{ki}|\, u_i}{\sum_{i} |\phi_{ki}|},
\qquad
EC_k \;=\; \lVert C_k \rVert \in [0, 1].
$$
$EC_k$ near $1$ means the prediction is driven by one coherent direction in
feature space; near $0$ means many competing contributions. `svconcentration()`
returns the coordinates, the angle, the dominant feature and $EC$;
`plot(type = "compass")` draws each observation as a point at $C_k$.

```{r compass, eval = have_gallery, fig.height = 5}
head(svconcentration(svb))
plot(svb, type = "compass")
```

## Fingerprint

A radial signature of $|\phi_{ki}|$ across features, drawn per observation or
per k-means cluster of the SHAP profiles $\{\phi_{k\cdot}\}$. It shows *which
shape* of explanation recurs in the data.

```{r fingerprint, eval = have_gallery, fig.height = 3.2}
plot(svb, type = "fingerprint", k = 4)
```

## Pathway

An alluvial of the top-`rank` contributors per observation: each node is a
feature, flow width is the number of observations sharing that ranked
contributor, and flow colour is the sign of the dominant contribution. Rare
pathways (fewer than `min_n` observations) are dropped. Needs `ggalluvial`.

```{r pathway, eval = have_alluvial, fig.height = 4}
plot(svb, type = "pathway", rank = 3)
```

# One colour system

Every plot draws its colours from `svstyle()`: the package's own diverging
pair `"shapvalues"`, or a `viridisLite` map (`"viridis"`, `"magma"`,
`"inferno"`, `"plasma"`, `"cividis"`). Structural elements (axes, separators)
stay constant across styles. Set it globally with `svstyle()` or per call
with the `style` argument; `svpalette()` returns the active colours.

```{r styles, eval = have_gallery, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "48%"}
plot(svb, type = "beeswarm", max_features = 6, title = "shapvalues")
plot(svb, type = "beeswarm", max_features = 6, title = "plasma", style = "plasma")
```

# Notes on accuracy and cost

* **More permutations.** The standard error of $\hat\phi_i$ is
  $O(M^{-1/2})$. For tree ensembles the estimate keeps moving until `nsim` is
  in the low hundreds; for additive models `nsim >= bg_size` is already exact.
* **Background size.** `bg_size` controls how well $v(S)$ approximates the
  conditioning expectation. Larger backgrounds reduce bias at linear cost in
  predictions.
* **Threads.** `nthreads` parallelises the reduction. Its effect is modest
  for single-output models (the batched predict and the R-side row assembly
  dominate) and largest for many-output classification.

individual predictions with feature contributions. *Knowledge and Information
Systems* 41(3), 647-665. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10115-013-0679-x>

Lundberg, S. M., Erion, G., Chen, H., DeGrave, A., Prutkin, J. M., Nair, B.,
Katz, R., Himmelfarb, J., Bansal, N. and Lee, S.-I. (2020). From local
explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees. *Nature
Machine Intelligence* 2, 56-67. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0138-9>

Krzyzinski, M., Spytek, M., Baniecki, H. and Biecek, P. (2023). SurvSHAP(t):
time-dependent explanations of machine learning survival models.
*Knowledge-Based Systems* 262, 110234. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2022.110234>
